docs.title: How Computers Play Chess
docs.text: A short, hands-on course. You will build a tiny chess engine in about 70 lines of Python, then see how it connects to Stockfish, AlphaZero and large language models.

docs.title: The big idea
docs.text:
A chess engine does two things:

  1. Search: look ahead through possible moves and replies.
  2. Evaluate: decide how good a position is when you stop looking.

Everything else, from bitboards to neural networks, makes one of these two faster or smarter.

docs.title: Course map
docs.text: Part Question it answers 1. Boards and moves How does a program know what's legal? 2. Judging a position How do you turn a position into a number? 3. Looking ahead How do you choose a move assuming the opponent plays well? 4. Pruning the tree How do you skip 99% of the work? 5. Modern engines What do Stockfish and Leela do differently? 6. LLMs and chess Can a language model play chess?

docs.title: Representing a position
docs.text:
A position needs: piece placement, side to move, castling rights, en passant square, and move counters. The standard text form is FEN:

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQKBNR w KQkq - 0 1

Ranks run from 8 down to 1. Digits are runs of empty squares. Uppercase is White.

docs.title: Bitboards
docs.text:
Serious engines store each piece type as a 64-bit integer, one bit per square. White pawns on their starting rank:

00000000 00000000 00000000 00000000 00000000 00000000 11111111 00000000

Moving every pawn forward one square is a single shift: pawns << 8. Checking which squares a rook attacks uses lookup tables and bit tricks. This is why engines search millions of positions per second.

Why 64 bits?

A chessboard has 64 squares, so a 64-bit word covers it exactly. CPUs operate on whole words in one instruction, so you process all 64 squares at once.

docs.title: Generating moves
docs.text:
We'll use the python-chess library, which handles the rules for us:

import chess

board = chess.Board()
print(board.legal_moves.count())   # 20
for move in board.legal_moves:
    print(board.san(move), end=" ")

docs.title: Perft: testing a move generator
docs.text:
Perft counts every leaf position reachable in exactly n moves. The right answers are well known, so any bug in move generation shows up as a wrong number.

"""Perft: count leaf positions at a given depth. A classic move-generator test."""
import chess


def perft(board: chess.Board, depth: int) -> int:
    if depth == 0:
        return 1
    total = 0
    for move in board.legal_moves:
        board.push(move)
        total += perft(board, depth - 1)
        board.pop()
    return total


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for d in range(1, 5):
        print(d, perft(chess.Board(), d))

Output:

Depth Positions 1 20 2 400 3 8,902 4 197,281 5 4,865,609

The count grows by about 20-30x per ply. That growth is the central problem of computer chess.

Experiment

Run perft from the position after 1. e4. Predict the depth-1 count first. Then try the position r3k2r/p1ppqpb1/bn2pnp1/3PN3/1p2P3/2N2Q1p/PPPBBPPP/R3K2R w KQkq - 0 1 (famous as "Kiwipete") and look up its known counts online.

docs.title: 2. Judging a position
docs.text: When the search stops, the engine needs a number: who's better, and by how much? This is the evaluation function. Scores are in centipawns, where 100 is roughly one pawn.

docs.title: Material
docs.text:
The classic starting point:

Piece Value Pawn 100 Knight 320 Bishop 330 Rook 500 Queen 900

Material alone already plays recognizable chess, but it makes poor choices when nothing can be captured.

docs.title: Piece-square tables
docs.text:
Where a piece stands matters. A knight in the centre attacks up to 8 squares, while a knight on the rim attacks 4 or fewer ("a knight on the rim is dim"). A piece-square table gives each square a bonus or penalty:

KNIGHT_TABLE = [
    -50, -40, -30, -30, -30, -30, -40, -50,
    -40, -20,   0,   5,   5,   0, -20, -40,
    ...
]

For Black we look up the mirrored square, so one table serves both colours.

docs.title: Negamax convention
docs.text:
Our evaluation returns the score from the side to move's point of view. This lets the search use a single function for both players, which part 3 explains.

def evaluate(board: chess.Board) -> int:
    """Score in centipawns from the point of view of the side to move."""
    if board.is_checkmate():
        return -MATE
    if board.is_stalemate() or board.is_insufficient_material():
        return 0
    score = 0
    for square, piece in board.piece_map().items():
        value = PIECE_VALUES[piece.piece_type]
        if piece.piece_type == chess.KNIGHT:
            idx = square if piece.color == chess.WHITE else chess.square_mirror(square)
            value += KNIGHT_TABLE[idx]
        score += value if piece.color == chess.WHITE else -value
    return score if board.turn == chess.WHITE else -score

Note

The full file is shown in part 4. The snippet above is the evaluate function.

docs.title: What real engines add
docs.text:
Beyond material and squares, classical evaluations score pawn structure (doubled, isolated, passed pawns), king safety, mobility, bishop pairs, and rooks on open files. Stockfish today replaces most of this with a neural network (see part 5).

Experiment

Set every knight-table value to 0 and compare the engine's opening moves with the original. Does it still develop knights toward the centre?

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
You choose the move that leads to the best outcome assuming your opponent also chooses their best reply. White tries to maximise the score, Black tries to minimise it.

        White to move
       /      |       \
     Ma       Mb       Mc          <- White picks the max
    /  \     /  \     /  \
  +3   +1   +2   +5  -2   +4       <- Black replies; Black picks the min

Black would answer Ma with +1 (the min of 3, 1), Mb with +2, and Mc with -2. White picks the best of those: Mb, worth +2.

docs.title: Negamax: one function for both sides
docs.text:
Because chess is zero-sum, one player's score is the negative of the other's. So we can write a single function:

\[\text{score}(p) = \max_{m}\; -\text{score}(p \cdot m)\]

Each recursion flips the sign. No separate max and min branches.

docs.title: Plain minimax in code
docs.text:
def minimax_nodes(board, depth):
    if depth == 0 or board.is_game_over():
        return evaluate(board), 1
    best, nodes = -MATE - 1, 1
    for move in board.legal_moves:
        board.push(move)
        score, n = minimax_nodes(board, depth - 1)
        board.pop()
        best, nodes = max(best, -score), nodes + n
    return best, nodes

docs.title: The problem: explosion
docs.text:
With about 30 legal moves per position, looking d plies ahead visits roughly \(30^d\) positions:

Depth Nodes (approx.) 2 900 4 810,000 6 729,000,000 8 656,000,000,000

Our plain minimax measured 775,804 nodes at depth 4. That's about what the formula predicts, and far too slow to go deeper.

Experiment

Run compare_search.py at depth 5. How long does plain minimax take compared with depth 4? That ratio is your effective branching factor.

docs.title: The insight
docs.text:
Suppose you've found a move that guarantees you +2. Now you examine another move and discover that the opponent has a reply that holds you to +1. You can stop looking at that move immediately. It's already worse than what you have, and it doesn't matter by how much.

Alpha-beta tracks two bounds:

  • alpha: the best score I can already guarantee.
  • beta: the best score the opponent can already guarantee. If my score reaches beta, the opponent would never allow this line, so I stop.
if alpha >= beta:   # the opponent would never allow this line
    break

docs.title: Move ordering matters
docs.text: Pruning works best when you examine the best moves first. If the first move is the best, every other branch gets cut quickly. Our engine orders captures first, using MVV-LVA (most valuable victim, least valuable attacker). Real engines add killer moves, history heuristics, and the best move from the previous, shallower search.

docs.title: The whole engine
docs.text:
"""A tiny chess engine: material + piece-square evaluation, negamax with alpha-beta."""
import chess

PIECE_VALUES = {
    chess.PAWN: 100, chess.KNIGHT: 320, chess.BISHOP: 330,
    chess.ROOK: 500, chess.QUEEN: 900, chess.KING: 0,
}

# Bonus (centipawns) for a white knight on each square, a1..h8. Mirrored for black.
KNIGHT_TABLE = [
    -50, -40, -30, -30, -30, -30, -40, -50,
    -40, -20,   0,   5,   5,   0, -20, -40,
    -30,   5,  10,  15,  15,  10,   5, -30,
    -30,   0,  15,  20,  20,  15,   0, -30,
    -30,   5,  15,  20,  20,  15,   5, -30,
    -30,   0,  10,  15,  15,  10,   0, -30,
    -40, -20,   0,   0,   0,   0, -20, -40,
    -50, -40, -30, -30, -30, -30, -40, -50,
]

MATE = 100_000


def evaluate(board: chess.Board) -> int:
    """Score in centipawns from the point of view of the side to move."""
    if board.is_checkmate():
        return -MATE
    if board.is_stalemate() or board.is_insufficient_material():
        return 0
    score = 0
    for square, piece in board.piece_map().items():
        value = PIECE_VALUES[piece.piece_type]
        if piece.piece_type == chess.KNIGHT:
            idx = square if piece.color == chess.WHITE else chess.square_mirror(square)
            value += KNIGHT_TABLE[idx]
        score += value if piece.color == chess.WHITE else -value
    return score if board.turn == chess.WHITE else -score


def ordered_moves(board: chess.Board):
    """Captures first (most valuable victim, least valuable attacker) to help pruning."""
    def key(move):
        if board.is_capture(move):
            victim = board.piece_type_at(move.to_square) or chess.PAWN  # en passant
            attacker = board.piece_type_at(move.from_square)
            return -(10 * PIECE_VALUES[victim] - PIECE_VALUES[attacker])
        return 0
    return sorted(board.legal_moves, key=key)


def negamax(board: chess.Board, depth: int, alpha: int, beta: int, stats: dict) -> int:
    stats["nodes"] += 1
    if depth == 0 or board.is_game_over():
        return evaluate(board)
    best = -MATE - 1
    for move in ordered_moves(board):
        board.push(move)
        score = -negamax(board, depth - 1, -beta, -alpha, stats)
        board.pop()
        best = max(best, score)
        alpha = max(alpha, score)
        if alpha >= beta:  # the opponent would never allow this line
            break
    return best


def best_move(board: chess.Board, depth: int = 3):
    stats = {"nodes": 0}
    best, best_score = None, -MATE - 1
    alpha, beta = -MATE - 1, MATE + 1
    for move in ordered_moves(board):
        board.push(move)
        score = -negamax(board, depth - 1, -beta, -alpha, stats)
        board.pop()
        if score > best_score:
            best, best_score = move, score
        alpha = max(alpha, score)
    return best, best_score, stats["nodes"]


if __name__ == "__main__":
    board = chess.Board()
    while not board.is_game_over() and board.fullmove_number < 20:
        move, score, nodes = best_move(board, depth=3)
        print(f"{board.fullmove_number}. {board.san(move)}  eval={score:+}  nodes={nodes}")
        board.push(move)
    print(board)

docs.title: Same answer, far less work
docs.text:
Running compare_search.py from the repo:

Depth Plain minimax Alpha-beta Same score? 1 28 28 yes 2 863 188 yes 3 24,942 1,258 yes 4 775,804 9,500 yes

At depth 4, alpha-beta visits about 1.2% of the nodes and returns exactly the same result. The savings grow with depth. With perfect ordering, alpha-beta searches about \(\sqrt{N}\) nodes, so it can look twice as deep in the same time.

docs.title: Why does it play oddly?
docs.text:
Run tiny_engine.py and watch the moves. It grabs material and then shuffles rooks around. That's expected: with only material and a knight table, once nothing can be won within three plies, every quiet move scores the same.

Experiment

Add a pawn advancement bonus (e.g. +5 per rank) to evaluate. Does the engine stop shuffling? Next, try depth 4 and see how long a move takes.

docs.title: What engines add on top
docs.text:
• Iterative deepening: search depth 1, then 2, then 3, and so on. It sounds wasteful, but the earlier results improve move ordering, and you can stop whenever time runs out.
  • Transposition table: cache positions you've already analysed, since different move orders reach the same position.
  • Quiescence search: don't stop in the middle of a capture sequence. Keep searching captures until the position is quiet.
  • Null-move pruning and late-move reductions: search unpromising moves less deeply.

docs.title: Stockfish: search plus a small neural net
docs.text:
Stockfish is still an alpha-beta engine at heart. Since 2020 it evaluates positions with NNUE (Efficiently Updatable Neural Network).

  • The network is small and runs on a CPU, no GPU needed.
  • It's efficiently updatable: when one piece moves, only a few input neurons change, so the first layer is updated incrementally instead of being recomputed.
  • It's trained on millions of positions scored by deep searches.

The result is a hand-written search paired with a learned evaluation, running at tens of millions of nodes per second.

docs.title: AlphaZero and Leela: learning from self-play
docs.text:
DeepMind's AlphaZero (2017) took a different path:

Stockfish AlphaZero / Leela Search Alpha-beta Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) Evaluation Small NNUE net Large deep network Hardware CPU GPU / TPU Nodes per second Tens of millions Tens of thousands Learning Trained on engine-scored positions Reinforcement learning via self-play from scratch

AlphaZero received only the rules. After a few hours of playing itself, it beat Stockfish 8. The open-source project Leela Chess Zero (Lc0) reproduced the approach with volunteer compute.

docs.title: MCTS in one paragraph
docs.text: Instead of searching every move to a fixed depth, MCTS repeatedly walks down the tree, preferring moves the network thinks are promising (the policy) and moves it hasn't tried much. At a leaf, the network gives a position value (the value). That value flows back up the tree. Over thousands of simulations, the most-visited move becomes the choice.

docs.title: The two networks, in short
docs.text:
• Policy head: "which moves look worth considering?" This replaces move ordering.
  • Value head: "who's winning?" This replaces the hand-written evaluation.

Pattern worth noticing

Both engines pair a search with a learned estimate. The difference is how much weight each side carries. Stockfish leans on brute-force search with a small net, while Leela leans on a big net with a lean search. The same trade-off shows up across modern AI.

docs.title: Strength today
docs.text: Top engines are rated well above 3500 Elo, while the best human is around 2800-2900. A phone running Stockfish beats every human alive.

docs.title: Can a language model play chess?
docs.text:
A language model predicts the next token. A game is just text, so you can feed it moves in PGN notation:

1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. Bb5

and ask for the next move. This works surprisingly well for the opening, because it has seen thousands of games and the opening theory in text form.

docs.title: Where it breaks down
docs.text:
Issue Why Illegal moves The model has no board state. It tracks the position implicitly from the move text. Blunders in tactics No search. It can't verify "if I go here, they take my queen". Long games drift Errors accumulate and the model can lose track of where pieces are.

Some research has shown that models trained on game transcripts build an internal representation of the board. The Othello-GPT work found that a network trained only on move sequences developed a board-state representation, even though it was never shown the board.

docs.title: Better: use the model as a coach, not a player
docs.text:
The reliable pattern is to let each tool do what it's good at:

engine  ->  finds the best move and the evaluation  (search)
LLM     ->  explains *why* in plain language         (language)

For example, feed Stockfish's analysis of a game (evaluation swings, best lines) to an LLM and ask it to explain the turning points. This is a good project for your own PGN files.

docs.title: Project idea: analyse your own games
docs.text:
1. Read your PGN files with python-chess.
  2. For each move, compute the evaluation with our tiny engine (or Stockfish via chess.engine).
  3. Flag moves where the evaluation drops by 150+ centipawns (blunders).
  4. Send each flagged position and the better move to an LLM and ask for a short explanation.
import chess.pgn, chess.engine

with open("game.pgn") as f:
    game = chess.pgn.read_game(f)

engine = chess.engine.SimpleEngine.popen_uci("stockfish")
board = game.board()
for move in game.mainline_moves():
    before = engine.analyse(board, chess.engine.Limit(depth=12))["score"].white()
    board.push(move)
    after = engine.analyse(board, chess.engine.Limit(depth=12))["score"].white()
    print(board.fullmove_number, move, before, "->", after)

Tip

You need the Stockfish binary installed (sudo apt install stockfish) for the snippet above. Check the path with which stockfish.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text: Roughly in order of difficulty.

docs.title: Warm-up
docs.text:
1. Run perft.py to depth 5. How long does it take? Estimate depth 6 from the growth rate.
  2. Change PIECE_VALUES so a bishop is worth 300 instead of 330. Does the opening choice change?
  3. Print the evaluation of the starting position. Why is it 0?

docs.title: Intermediate
docs.text:
1. Add piece-square tables for pawns and the king. For the king, use different tables for the middlegame and the endgame.
  2. Implement iterative deepening with a time limit, and return the best move found so far.
  3. Add a transposition table using chess.polyglot.zobrist_hash(board) as the key. Measure the node reduction.
  4. Add quiescence search: at depth 0, keep searching captures until none remain. Test with a position where a queen can be captured by a pawn at the horizon.

docs.title: Challenge
docs.text:
1. Play your engine against Stockfish limited to Skill Level 0 using chess.engine. Play 20 games and estimate the win rate.
  2. Build the LLM coach from part 6 for your own games.
  3. Train a tiny evaluation network: generate positions from random games, label them with Stockfish at depth 8, and fit a small PyTorch MLP. Compare it with the hand-written evaluation.

Where this leads

Exercise 10 is the core of how NNUE works. Once you've done it, you understand the main idea behind modern engines.
